name: Muti

card.summary: Southern African traditional medicine (umuthi), prepared by herbalists and diviners, including remedies and charms for protection, fortune and well-being.
card.note: Some preparations are toxic; criminal 'muti murders' involve body parts and are condemned by traditional healer groups.

quick.overview:
Muti, from the Zulu and Xhosa word umuthi meaning tree, is the Southern African term for traditional medicines, usually plant-based, prescribed by healers such as inyangas (herbalists) and sangomas (diviners). The wiki covers it because muti traditions include remedies and charms for protection, well-being and success, and plant preparations for skin and body care.

It is a large part of everyday health care in the region: Wikipedia cites an estimated 200,000 traditional healers in South Africa, with around 60 percent of the population consulting them, usually alongside conventional medicine.
quick.how: Clients consult an inyanga or sangoma, who may prescribe infusions, decoctions, snuffs, washes or charms made from plants, animal parts or minerals, often bought at muti markets. Treatment is tied to diagnosis, which for sangomas may include divination and ancestral guidance.
quick.risks: Some plant preparations can be toxic and are unregulated in dose. A separate, criminal practice known as muti murder involves the killing of people for body parts; traditional healer groups and governments condemn it. South Africa recognises traditional health practitioners under the Traditional Health Practitioners Act of 2007.

lead: Muti (also muthi) is the term in South African English for traditional medicine in Southern Africa, reaching north as far as Lake Tanganyika. [1] It comes from the Zulu, Xhosa and Northern Ndebele word umuthi, meaning tree, and usually refers to botanical remedies prescribed by an inyanga, though it can also include animal and mineral preparations. [1]

Traditional healers are divided into inyangas, who work mainly with plant and animal medicines, and sangomas, diviners who practise ngoma, a belief system centred on ancestral spirits; muthi is described as medicine imbued with spiritual significance. [2] Wikipedia estimates around 200,000 traditional healers in South Africa versus about 25,000 biomedically trained doctors, and roughly 60 percent of South Africans consult traditional healers, usually alongside biomedical services. [2]

Muti is used for protection, pregnancy and childcare, and wound care; in popular usage in South Africa and in Afrikaans, the word can also mean any medicine or something seen as miraculous. [1] People seeking appearance or attraction benefits from muti are describing charms and washes within this broader tradition, and published research on such uses is limited.

angle.text: Within muti traditions, healers prescribe remedies and charms for health, protection and success, and some plant preparations are used on the skin. Appearance effects are not a formal focus of the tradition and are claimed rather than studied.

paras: Muti covers botanical remedies and, less often, zoological and mineral preparations, prescribed by traditional healers. [1] Plants are central: traditional medicine uses about 3,000 of Southern Africa's roughly 30,000 higher plant species. [2] Examples include Gazania linearis applied to small cuts as protection against evil spirits, and Chlorophytum comosum as a protective charm for mother and child. [1]

Plants classed as isicakathi in Xhosa are mostly used by pregnant women and children and for protection during pregnancy, and Agapanthus praecox is used in pre- and post-natal care. [1] Impepho (Helichrysum petiolare) is burned in summoning rituals. [2]

Inyangas prescribe herbal and animal medicines; sangomas diagnose through divination and ancestral spirits. [2] Grokipedia describes apprenticeships under senior instructors and muti markets in cities such as Johannesburg. [3]

South Africa's Traditional Health Practitioners Act of 2007 legally recognises sangomas as traditional health practitioners and provides for a national council to regulate and register them; an interim council was inaugurated in February 2013 and several sections took effect in May 2014. An earlier 2004 act was ruled unconstitutional. [2]

Muti killings are murders in which body parts are removed for use in traditional medicines and rituals; Wikipedia says they are not human sacrifices in the direct sense. [1] In July 1983 Eswatini executed Philippa Mdluli, convicted of a 1980 child murder during a muti ritual, and in February 2010 African traditional healers and the Gauteng government met in Pretoria to address the 'evil practice of mutilating human bodies for purposes of muti making.' [1]

The wiki does not treat these crimes as part of muti healing; healer organisations and authorities treat them as crimes, and the motive in one reported case was to make a business more successful. [1]

Published research includes a 1988 study by Bolofo and Johnson identifying eleven isicakathi species in the Transkei and a 2002 study by Abrahams and colleagues on indigenous healing and self-medication among pregnant women in Cape Town. [1] Wikipedia notes that no traditional medicine in South Africa has been clinically proven to treat HIV/AIDS. [2]
No studies found on muti as a whole; research is limited to ethnobotanical and survey studies of individual plants and healer use. [1]
